newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Salinas says brother must explain fortune.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Salinas says brother must explain fortune.

text.p: Former Mexican President Carlos Salinas admitted in an interview published on Thursday that his brother Raul had "hurt the people" of Mexico by piling up a multi-million dollar fortune, but he denied that Raul had arranged the murder of a top politician.

Raul Salinas was arrested and jailed three months after his brother, on charges of ordering the September 1994 killing of the ruling party's secretary general, Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, his former brother-in-law.
A few days later Carlos Salinas fled Mexico to live abroad in Dublin, Ireland. He travels often to the United States to visit his old school, Harvard, and to attend meetings of the Dow Jones board.

"I am convinced of the innocence of my brother," Salinas said in the second part of a wide-ranging interview with the Mexican daily Reforma, conducted in Boston. "No credible motive (for Raul ordering the murder) has been proven ... the accusation which was finally used to arrest my brother ... was made after what has been reported as a bribe of half a million dollars which (the witness) was given."

Prosecutors have charged Raul Salinas with illicit enrichment after finding foreign bank accounts containing several hundred million dollars, most of which was apparently accumulated toward the end of his brother's administration.

"That behaviour of my brother Raul has hurt me deeply," Salinas said. "It has hurt my brothers and it has also hurt my government. But above all, it has hurt the people and that is why he must explain it and cast light on it."

Salinas said he had no idea Raul was piling up such a large fortune but he conceded that he should have paid more attention to his brother's activities. "I admit, looking at everything that we have gone through, that I should not have allowed myself that lack of attention," he said.
Asked what he would do with Raul's fortune, Salinas said: "Apply the law and if its origin is illicit, seize it."
He also denied news reports that he had been told of the existence of an Indian guerrilla group long before the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN) launched its armed uprising on Jan. 1, 1994.
